schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'the house of Haman' as all that pertained to it and mark Mordecai coming before the king as Esther's kinsman and foster-father (Esther 2:7); Ellicott notes confiscation followed a death-sentence in the East.

Clarke: Haman's treason forfeited life and goods, justly conferred on Mordecai who had saved the king; Wesley: the estate bestowed on Esther to compensate her danger, Mordecai made one of the seven princes.
Henry: Esther enriched — the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just (Prov. 13:22); Mordecai advanced, so humble he had concealed the relation and never used her interest.
Gill: the house and estate confiscated to the crown and given to Esther, who would have been the sufferer; the Targum adds all his treasures.

themes: the house of Haman given to Esther
the wealth of the sinner for the just

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the seal-ring taken from Haman (Esther 3:10) advances Mordecai to first minister, as Joseph in Gen. 41:42, the seal giving edicts the force of law; Ellicott: the ring makes him vizier, his place now what Daniel's was to Darius.

Clarke: giving the ring was giving the seal of the kingdom, constituting Mordecai a lord chancellor; Wesley: with the ring goes the power it signifies, and Esther sets him as steward over Haman's estate.
Gill: the ring, a Persian token of the strongest friendship, made Mordecai keeper of the seals.

Keil and Delitzsch: the chief enemy dead, but the sealed edict still stood irrevocable by Persian law, so Esther wept at the king's feet to do away Haman's device; Ellicott: her work half done, she grows bolder to ask what lay beyond the king's own power.
Henry: a man's mischief survives him; she wept for her people though not for her own life — tears of pity are the most Christ-like, and it was time to be earnest when the church was at stake.
Gill: she came uncalled a second time with a new petition.

themes: the sealed edict still in force
earnest for the church at stake

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the king held out the sceptre and Esther rose from his feet to stand as petitioner; Ellicott refers back to the law of Esther 4:11 that made the gesture a matter of life and death.
Gill: the sceptre held out was the token that she had not incurred displeasure and was admitted to speak.
Henry: she was encouraged to present her petition by the king's holding out the golden sceptre.

Keil and Delitzsch: the introductory formulas strengthened for so weighty a matter; Ellicott admires her skill — 'to reverse' is 'to bring back,' and she names the device as Haman's, not the king's, letters.
Wesley: her heaped phrases confirm the king's favour by full submission, prudently laying the hatefulness on Haman, who had circumvented the king.
Gill: the heap of phrases is used to work on the king's affections and to show her submission.
Henry: soft askings obtain favour as soft answers turn away wrath; even with justice on our side we should petition superiors with modesty.

themes: guilt laid on Haman not the king

schools.summary: Gill: 'I cannot bear it' — she names not oppression but extermination, and calls them her kindred, of the same family.
Keil and Delitzsch: the king, moved by her plea and unable simply to revoke the edict, first assures her of his good intentions before granting the remedy.
Clarke: having owned herself Mordecai's cousin and so a Jewess, she pleads that though she and Mordecai were safe, the decree still doomed her people.
Henry: a queen owning her poor kindred, weeping for her people though not for her own life — she will not be delivered alone.

themes: how can I endure to see the evil
the plea that moves the king

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the king cannot revoke the edict but reminds them he gave Haman's house to Esther and hanged Haman for laying hand on the Jews, as preface to the permission; Ellicott: he points to these proofs of goodwill before doing what he can.
Gill: Mordecai now present in the audience, one of those who saw the king's face.
Henry: the king had shown his concern by hanging his favourite, and now leaves his name and power with Esther and Mordecai as he once left it with Haman.

themes: the king addresses Esther and Mordecai
Haman hanged for touching the Jews

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: leave granted, as once to Haman, to write in the king's name and seal with his ring 'as seems good to you' to render the edict harmless; Ellicott: repeal declined, but the difficulty met by authorising self-defence.

Clarke: no sealed edict could be repealed, but a matching one could arm the Jews on an equal footing; Wesley marvels at so rigid a law and prefers a constitution where none is unrepealable — God alone cannot repent.
Gill: 'write as it liketh you' — whatever is fit for their safety and security.
Henry: the irrevocable-decree law (cf. Dan. 6:15) is pride and folly, 'we will be as gods'; the expedient forced a civil war waged by the king's authority yet against it.

themes: the law that may not be reversed
arming the Jews to equal footing

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the letters written on 23 Sivan per Mordecai's command to the 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, each in its own language; Ellicott dates Sivan to May, more than two months after the first edict.
Gill: the king's scribes called, as for the former letter.
Wesley: God suffered the two-month delay to humble the Jews and rebuke their neglect of returning to their land, and to magnify the deliverance.
Henry: the decree published in every province's own language — shall subjects have the king's decrees in a tongue they understand while God's oracles are locked in an unknown one?

outliers.note: Reads the two-month interval of terror as a deliberate chastening — that the scattered Jews might be humbled and purged and rebuked for having declined to return to their own land — a providential purpose the other witnesses do not draw.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: written in the king's name, sealed, sent by posts on horseback and swift beasts; Ellicott: 'posts' are 'runners,' the animals horses of great speed (Micah 1:13), the doubtful words rendered royal-bred mules or coursers of the king's stud.

Clarke owns the beasts' names incurably uncertain — swift chariot-horses or large mules — but of little importance, only the swiftest available; Wesley: these riders, not used before, were added for speed to ease the Jews' fears.
Gill: written in the king's name and sealed with his ring, giving authority and making it irreversible.

Clarke: the decree's words match Haman's, giving the Jews equal authority; the women-and-children clause was formal parity, the custom of destroying a convict's family; Wesley: it was added to strike terror, yet no slaughter of women or children is recorded.
Ellicott: the Jews were licensed only to stand on the defensive; though empowered to take spoil, when the day came they declined it.
Gill: the Jews granted to gather in a body, sufficiently armed, in every city.
Henry: commissioned to gather for defence on the very day of their intended ruin — the latter decree a tacit revocation of the former.
Gill: the thirteenth of Adar was the very day fixed in the former letters for the Jews' destruction.
Keil and Delitzsch: the same day, one day in all the provinces, now given to the Jews to stand and be avenged.
Henry: they were to gather for defence on the very day appointed for their ruin — the trap turned.
Wesley: the decree went out more than two months after the first, and the day it named still lay months off, leaving time to prepare.

themes: the day of doom made the day of deliverance
one day in all the provinces
the letter of doom left standing

schools.summary: Gill: the decree published by herald and posted in public places, that all might know and not dare assault the Jews.
Ellicott (with Wordsworth): 'to avenge' signifies not resentful passion but a steady resolve to defend the right, a word used even of the Almighty rescuing the oppressed.
Henry: the Jews empowered to stand ready against the day of assault, that the attack might break upon them.
Ellicott asks why such haste with nine months to spare, and answers: fear lest the first edict's animus embolden eager partisans to anticipate the date.
Clarke: the decree given at Shushan, in every respect the mirror of the former, only its effect the contrary.
Gill: the posts rode out on the swift royal beasts, carrying the decree from the capital.
Henry: hastened by the king's own command as well as Mordecai's, the king in pain lest the news come too late.

themes: chasing down the word of death

schools.summary: Clarke describes the robes and turban and byssus, noting Haman was too proud to be popular; Wesley: the great crown such as chief princes wore, and the citizens who by nature abhorred bloody counsels rejoiced in mercy.
Henry: Mordecai in purple and the Jews in joy — the ensigns of dignity made ornaments of piety; when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice.
Gill: Mordecai went out to show himself to his friends.
Ellicott notes the crown is not the royal diadem, and reads the city's cheer cynically — a fickle mob shouting with the winning side, like the crowd that cried Hosanna then Crucify.

debates.question: Why did the city of Shushan rejoice at Mordecai's exaltation?

sides.position: honest relief and a love of mercy — joy at the triumph of virtue
the fickle cheer of a crowd that shouts with the winning side

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: 'light' a rare figure for prosperity, 'honour' the esteem shown in the general joy at the prevention of their destruction.
Gill: 'light' is prosperity against the darkness of adversity, a lightsomeness of spirit explained by the words that follow.
Wesley: the piled synonyms denote the greatness of the joy — honour now instead of contempt.
Henry: sowing in tears to reap in joy, like those that dream (Ps. 126:1) — the sudden turn only heightening their gladness.

Keil and Delitzsch: joy and feasting where Haman's edict had brought lamentation, and many became Jews — not, Keil judges, merely for security, but the greater number from more than fear; Ellicott: they embraced the religion as proselytes.
Clarke: converts for fear are unlikely to honour true religion; the historian states only that they professed Judaism for fear, whether they held to it or not.
Henry: many sober, well-inclined people were proselyted and renounced their idols; Haman meant to extirpate the Jews, and their numbers were increased — holy joy invites others in.

debates.question: Were the many conversions to Judaism genuine?

sides.position: fearful, time-serving professions of doubtful sincerity
a real turning to God and a providential ingathering

outliers.note: Turns the fear-driven conversions into a maxim that only the Gospel forbids coercion, being a spiritual kingdom propagated by spiritual means alone (John 18:36) — a homiletical excursus the other witnesses do not make.
